purpose: Isatuximab-irfc is used to treat multiple myeloma, which is a type of blood cancer that affects plasma cells in your bone marrow. It is typically used in combination with other cancer medicines when previous treatments have not worked well enough. It helps slow down or stop the growth of cancer cells.
how_it_works: This medicine is a specially designed protein called a monoclonal antibody that seeks out and attaches to a specific target called CD38, which is found in large amounts on multiple myeloma cancer cells. Once it locks onto those cancer cells, it signals your immune system to attack and destroy them. Think of it like a guided missile that helps your own body find and fight the cancer more effectively.
common_side_effects: Common side effects include infusion reactions during or shortly after your IV treatment such as chills, cough, shortness of breath, or feeling flushed. You may also experience fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, upper respiratory infections like colds, low blood cell counts, and pneumonia. Let your care team know if any of these bother you.
warnings: This medicine can cause serious infusion reactions, so you will be monitored closely during your infusions and given pre-medications beforehand to reduce the risk. It can lower your blood cell counts, increasing your risk of infections, anemia, and bleeding, so regular blood tests are important. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby. Also tell your lab team you are on this medicine because it can interfere with certain blood type testing.
typical_dosing: Isatuximab-irfc is given as an IV infusion in a clinic or hospital setting, not at home. A typical schedule starts with weekly infusions for the first month, then every two weeks after that. Your exact dose is calculated based on your body weight, and your doctor will determine the right schedule for you based on your treatment plan.
